title: How Ansarallah Swept Past Saudi-Backed Forces to Control Yemen’s Red Sea Coast
author: Iona Craig

loyal Yemen's Saudi-backed government stand near a pick-up truck in the Hays
district, south of Hodeidah on September 5, 2026. Photo by Khaled ZIAD / AFP
via Getty Images.

Yemen's Ansarallah completed their control of the Bab al-Mandab on Friday
following sweeping gains yesterday in the most significant shift in
territorial control in five years of the country's long-running civil war.

Following days of escalating fighting in the western mountains of Taiz
governorate, Saudi-backed forces of the Internationally Recognized Government
(IRG) of Yemen appeared to collapse on Thursday, allowing Ansarallah, also
known as the Houthis, to seize the strategically important port-city of Mocha.
On Friday, Ansarallah forces took Mayum island, also known as Perim, which
lies on the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait two miles off Yemen's west
coast. The small volcanic island acts as a natural choke point in the strait,
narrowing the Red Sea channel to nine miles from the coast of Djibouti.

Ansarallah fighters posted videos online of military vehicles driving down the
runway--built in 2022 by the United Arab Emirates--at Mocha's newly developed
airport. Footage also showed detainees being released from the city's central
prison as Ansarallah took control.

The advance puts the Houthis in direct control of one of the world's busiest
shipping lanes. Around one-third of international cargo shipping passes
through the strait, a route that has become increasingly important for oil
exports in the wake of the U.S. war on Iran, which has shut off access through
the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, hailed
what he called a "resounding victory" for Ansarallah. "Iran's might in the
Strait of Hormuz and the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the
U.S. and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse," he
[wrote](https://x.com/mokhberofficial/status/2098365602993705257?s=46) in a
social media post.

Saudi airstrikes were reported late on Thursday night and into Friday around
Dhubab and Mocha, hitting the port and airport.

Yemen's civil war, which had been largely dormant since a Houthi-Saudi
ceasefire was brokered in 2022, reignited in July when Saudi Arabia carried
out airstrikes on Sana'a airport to prevent an inbound Iranian passenger plane
from landing in the Houthi-controlled capital. The plane later touched down
safely in Hodeidah. The Mahan Air flight was the first passenger jet to land
in Houthi territory since Israel destroyed five commercial planes belonging to
Yemen's state airline Yemenia in May last year.

In response, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on all Saudi-linked
vessels, disrupting the Kingdom's export of oil to Asia from its Yanbu
terminal on the west coast that was exporting an average of 4 million barrels
of oil per day to bypass the closed Strait of Hormuz. Houthi attacks on Saudi
vessels followed, forcing the rerouting of Asian-bound oil tankers north
through the Suez Canal and the much longer route east via the Cape of Good
Hope.

The incident relaunched fighting on the ground between Iranian-allied
Ansarallah and the Saudi-backed IRG. The latter has been consolidating its
power under Saudi direction since the [sudden
withdrawal](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/yemen-uae-saudi-southern-
transitional-council) by the UAE of its forces and support for Yemen's anti-
Houthi Southern Transitional Council (STC) in January during a spectacular
falling out between the Kingdom and the Emirates.

Since the violent UAE-Saudi split at the beginning of the year, Saudi Arabia
has sought to consolidate its hold over the Yemeni government and armed
forces. A Yemeni Supreme Military Committee, created in January with the task
of unifying the multiple fighting units including those previously under UAE
command, is headed by Saudi commander Lieutenant General Mutlaq bin Salem Al-
Azima. But any attempts at cohesion appear to have failed.

Witnesses described to Drop Site armed men looting weapons, and combat
vehicles from retreating IRG forces heading into the suburb of Buraiqa, five
miles west of the Aden, highlighting the fractured nature of the anti-Houthi
side. Other fighters were
[filmed](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1362058839417569) selling their weapons
as they fled on the road east of Bab al-Mandab.

"They continue to grossly underestimate the capabilities of the Houthis,"
Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the London-based Chatham House's Middle
East and North Africa program, told Drop Site. "At the same time, there is a
fundamental problem of military coordination for the IRG forces."

Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of Yemen's
long-standing president Ali Abduallah Saleh, who was killed by the Houthis in
2017, were heading the fight against Ansarallah on the Red Sea coast until
their withdrawal on Thursday. Saleh and his fighters have subsequently been
[accused](https://www.facebook.com/reel/2953782088322647) of betrayal and
cowardice by Yemeni media channels and in social media[
posts](https://www.facebook.com/reel/955564883507174) by other fighters in the
Saudi-backed side.

Tareq Saleh's media office did not respond to Drop Site's request for comment
on Thursday's retreat.

A day earlier, the IRG Minister of Defense came under
[attack](https://www.facebook.com/reel/1709339656832618) from southern
fighters while visiting the frontline against the Houthis in Al-Dhale, the
home territory of UAE-backed STC leader Aidrous al-Zubeidi, who fled into
exile in January during the Saudi push back against the STC that
[ended](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/yemen-uae-saudi-southern-transitional-
council) the UAE's decade-long military presence in Yemen.

In the midst of Ansarallah's advances on Thursday, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed
bin Salaman[ reportedly](https://www.axios.com/2026/09/11/houthis-yemen-saudi-
trump-mbs-strikes) called President Trump twice to appeal for U.S. strikes
against the Houthis. Provisional numbers from airstrikes monitor Yemen Data
Project recorded 77 Saudi air raids between September 4 and 10, marking the
heaviest period of Saudi bombing on Yemen since early 2022.

The Houthis also stepped up attacks inside the Kingdom this week, launching a
wave of ballistic missiles and drones on Tuesday that hit state oil facilities
in Abha, Najran and Aramco's facility in Jizan resulting in 73 wounded
civilians, [according to](https://apnews.com/article/saudi-arabia-yemen-
houthis-4ad9446f0bb8c096750c84b6e1ba86b8) Saudi officials.

Residents in Aden, which remains under IRG control, told Drop Site News that
hundreds of displaced families were arriving in the city from the Red Sea
coastal towns and villages. At least 46,000 people have been displaced since
fighting escalated last week, according to new figures [released
](https://www.iom.int/news/displacement-yemen-alarmingly-surges-
past-46000-amid-escalating-fighting-iom-chief)on Friday by the International
Organization for Migration (IOM), up from 18,500 reported by IOM on Tuesday.

The price of crude oil, already rising to over $100 a barrel this week due to
the U.S.-Iran conflict over the Strait of Hormuz, jumped a further 6.5% on
Thursday following Ansarallah's territorial gains.

Rising oil prices are expected to have a further knock-on effect on borrowing
costs set by central banks. The European Central Bank[ put
up](https://apnews.com/article/europe-tariffs-economic-growth-trump-
de62b59fba535fccaf6f75e52d037c63) its interest rate by a quarter point on
Thursday. Bank President Christine Lagarde cited the region's instability in
the decision, saying in a press conference that "the conflict in the Middle
East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain
well above target for an extended period." The U.S. Federal Reserve is due to
announce its decision on rates next week.

Ansarallah officials sought to downplay any threat to shipping in the Bab al-
Mandab. Their Supreme Political Council released a[
statement](https://english.masirahtv.net/post/58016/Yemen-s-Supreme-Political-
Council-Reaffirms-Commitment-to-International-Navigation-Obligations) after
the gains on Thursday saying that "navigation in the Red Sea remains safe"
although Saudi vessels remain a target.

The Saudis are now forced into a whole new war with the Houthis, says Al-
Muslimi. "This is unprecedented and they can't let the Houthis get away with
attacks like this inside Saudi Arabia. The economic impact would be too huge
and it would set a precedent for anyone else who wants to attack them." As for
the international community and their response to the Houthi capture of the
Bab al-Mandab, Al-Muslimi added: "They are out of tools, time and
imagination."
